legend: Given a natural number n$$$n$$$, count the number of permutations (p1,p2,…,pn)$$$(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n)$$$ of the numbers from 1$$$1$$$ to n$$$n$$$, such that for each i$$$i$$$ (1≤i≤n$$$1 \le i \le n$$$), the following property holds: pi mod pi+1≤2$$$p_i \text{ mod } p_{i+1} \le 2$$$, where pn+1=p1$$$p_{n+1} = p_1$$$.
As this number can be very big, output it modulo 109+7$$$10^9 + 7$$$.
input: The only line of the input contains the integer n$$$n$$$ (1≤n≤106$$$1 \le n \le 10^6$$$).
output: Output a single integer — the number of the permutations satisfying the condition from the statement, modulo 109+7$$$10^9+7$$$.
note: For example, for n=4$$$n = 4$$$ you should count the permutation [4,2,3,1]$$$[4, 2, 3, 1]$$$, as 4 mod 2=0≤2$$$4 \text{ mod } 2 = 0 \leq 2$$$, 2 mod 3=2≤2$$$2 \text{ mod } 3 = 2 \leq 2$$$, 3 mod 1=0≤2$$$3 \text{ mod } 1 = 0 \leq 2$$$, 1 mod 4=1≤2$$$1 \text{ mod } 4 = 1 \leq 2$$$. However, you shouldn't count the permutation [3,4,1,2]$$$[3, 4, 1, 2]$$$, as 3 mod 4=3>2$$$3 \text{ mod } 4 = 3  \gt  2$$$ which violates the condition from the statement.
